title: Colombia's Fuzzy 'Water Guardians' Need Help
summary: High in the Andes Mountains of Colombia, at 10,000 feet above sea level, Moisés Moreno runs a greenhouse full of tiny seedlings. They may look small now, but they can grow to be 30 feet tall. They are frailejones, strange fuzzy plants that help supply water to millions of people. Frailejones are related to the sunflower, and they are the signature plants of the páramos, Colombia's high mountain wetlands. The woolly fuzz on their leaves protects them from the cold and soaks up water from the clouds. That moisture feeds the páramos, which are the source of major rivers and much of Colombia's water. When explorers first spotted the plants poking out of the mountain fog centuries ago, they thought they looked like hooded monks. That is how they got their name: frailejón means 'big friar' in Spanish. The Muisca people, who once lived in the area, considered frailejones sacred guardians of the water. But today, the plants are in trouble. Of the nearly 150 species of frailejones, two-thirds are at risk and 17 are endangered, says Mauricio Diazgranados, a Colombian plant expert at the New York Botanical Garden. Farmers, cattle ranchers, and coal miners are pushing higher into the mountains, and a warming climate is letting invasive species survive at altitudes where they could not before. Moreno knows the threats well. Growing up on a mountainside farm near the town of Monguí, he used to chop frailejones down to make room for potato fields and cow pastures. 'We viewed them as a nuisance,' he says. Later, while working in a coal mine, he was injured in a cave-in and decided to work above ground in the fresh mountain air. He began studying the páramo, started his greenhouse, and now leads tourists and volunteers on trips to replant the frailejones that were wiped out. The work is slow and uncertain. Volunteers hike to 11,000 feet, dig shallow holes, and nestle six-inch seedlings into the soil. Many die in the cold, harsh climate, and the ones that survive grow only a few inches a year. Still, the volunteers keep coming. Some have even given their seedlings names. Biologist Julieta Barba named hers 'Gerry,' after her mother. 'I'm very excited for her future here in the páramo,' she said after patting dirt around its roots. Colombia's National Parks agency and even its armed forces have joined reforestation efforts after wildfires scorched thousands of acres of frailejones. And many Colombians first learned about the plant from Ernesto Pérez, a hugely popular cartoon character shaped like a frailejon who urges people to protect the Andes, much like Smokey Bear promotes forest fire prevention in the United States.
why_it_matters: The páramos supply water to millions of people, so protecting the plants that keep them healthy protects drinking water too.

background_read: The páramos are high, cold, wet mountain lands in the Andes, and they act like giant sponges that soak up water from clouds and rain and release it slowly into rivers.
Frailejones are plants that grow only in these high places; their fuzzy leaves protect them from the cold and help them catch water from the mist.
When a plant is a keystone species, many other living things depend on it, so losing it can harm the whole ecosystem, including the water people drink.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Fuzzy frailejón plants help supply much of Colombia's water, and they are in trouble.
KEY EVENT: Volunteers are replanting frailejones high in the Andes.
├─ WHO: Moisés Moreno, volunteers, and plant expert Mauricio Diazgranados.
└─ WHEN: Now, with seedlings planted at 11,000 feet.
EVIDENCE: Two-thirds of nearly 150 species are at risk and 17 are endangered; seedlings grow only a few inches a year.
OPEN QUESTION: Can enough frailejones survive to protect the páramos?
